main.toolTipHeader: Pauza - The break time reminder app
main.warning: This will restore app defaults and all your settings will be lost.

settings.openAtLogin: Start Pauza automatically when logging in
settings.monitorIdleTime: Monitor system idle time (breaks are paused if system is idle).
settings.monitorDnd: Show breaks even in Do Not Disturb mode
settings.interruptionStyleInfo: Choose how assertively Pauza appears when a break starts.

schedule.miniBreaksInfo: Microbreaks are short breaks taken regularly to give you a chance to stretch and relax.
schedule.longBreaksInfo: Breaks are taken less regularly, but last longer, allowing you to step away from your work for a fuller reset.
schedule.strictModeInfo: Strict mode prevents you from skipping either Microbreaks or Breaks and is designed to help discipline.
schedule.cantDisableBoth: It is not possible to disable both types of breaks

about.learnMore: To learn more about Pauza features, view a tutorial, download the latest version or contact us for support,
about.designedBy: Icon and UI design by Colin Shanley

heart.desc1: Taking regular breaks when using a computer is scientifically proven to be important for your physical and mental well-being.
heart.desc2: Pauza is free. But you can lend your support by donating and help us continue to improve Pauza and release other free software.

contributorPreferences.title: Contributor Preferences
contributorPreferences.notificationsInfo: System notification shown before breaks to let you prepare for it.
contributorPreferences.newVersionNotification: Notify when new version is available
contributorPreferences.customIdeasInfo: Allows you to use custom break ideas by editing configuration file. (For advanced users.)
contributorPreferences.useIdeasFromSettings: Use break ideas from configuration file
contributorPreferences.breakPostponeInfo: If enabled in main Preferences, you can postpone breaks. Following settings allow you to specify when, for how long and how many times you can postpone a break.
contributorPreferences.pauseUntilMorningInfo: Specify till what hour 'Pause until morning' should pause.
contributorPreferences.showWelcomeWindow: Show Welcome window on next start
contributorPreferences.opacityInfo: How solid should the break window be?
contributorPreferences.breakWindowSizeInfo: What percentage of the screen should the break window hide?
contributorPreferences.miniBreakStartSound: Sound at the start of Microbreak
contributorPreferences.longBreakStartSound: Sound at the start of Break
contributorPreferences.naturalBreaksInfo: If monitoring of idle time is enabled in main Preferences, you can specify after what time the breaks should be paused.
contributorPreferences.showBreaksAsRegularWindowsInfo: When enabled, break windows will become focusable, they won't be 'Always on top' anymore and they will also appear in the taskbar.
contributorPreferences.screenInfo: When showing breaks on all monitors is disabled, you can choose which one you would like to show your breaks on.
contributorPreferences.showTimeToBreakInTray: Show time to next break in tray
contributorPreferences.showCurrentTimeInBreaks: Show current local time in break window

aaa.text: Go grab a glass of water.

aab.text: Your water bottle is judging you. Take a sip.

aac.text: Hydration check: when did you last drink water?

aad.text: Slowly look all the way left, then right.

aae.text: Slowly look all the way up, then down.

aaf.text: Look at something 6 meters away for 20 seconds — the 20-20-20 rule.

aag.text: Blink rapidly 20 times. Your dry eyes will thank you.

aah.text: Close your eyes and gently roll your eyeballs in circles.

aai.text: With your eyes closed, slowly look up toward the ceiling, then down.

aaj.text: With your eyes closed, slowly look left, then right.

aak.text: Rub your hands together until warm, then gently cup them over your closed eyes.

aal.text: Stare out the window for 30 seconds. Remember the outside world?

aam.text: Look away from the screen and focus on something green. Eyes love green.

aan.text: Let some natural light reach your eyes.

aao.text: Close your eyes and take a few deep breaths.

aaq.text: Close your eyes and count your breaths.

aar.text: Breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 7, exhale for 8. The 4-7-8 technique.

aas.text: Take 3 slow breaths. In through the nose, out through the mouth.

aat.text: Take one deep breath so big your belly expands. That's diaphragmatic breathing.

aau.text: Do absolutely nothing for 20 seconds. Harder than it sounds.

aav.text: Check your posture — shoulders back, feet flat on the floor.

aax.text: Drop your shoulders. They've been up by your ears this whole time.

aay.text: Unclench your jaw. You didn't realize it was clenched, did you?

aaz.text: Straighten your spine. Pretend there's a string pulling you up from the top of your head.

aba.text: Sitting is the new smoking. Stand up for a minute.

abb.text: Slowly turn your head to one side and hold for 10 seconds. Switch.

abc.text: Slowly tilt your head to the side and hold for 5-10 seconds.

abd.text: Gently pull one ear toward your shoulder. Feel the neck stretch.

abe.text: Rotate your neck in a slow, gentle circle.

abf.text: Tilt your head forward, backward, left, right. Full compass reset.

abg.text: Roll your shoulders forward for 10 seconds, then backward.

abh.text: Shrug your shoulders up to your ears and drop them. Repeat 5 times.

abi.text: Squeeze your shoulder blades together and hold for 5 seconds.

abj.text: Raise your right arm over your head, lean left, hold 10 seconds. Switch sides.

abk.text: Cross one arm across your chest and gently pull it in with the other hand. Switch.

abl.text: Hold one arm straight up, use the other to gently push the elbow back. Hold 10 seconds. Switch.

abm.text: Interlock your fingers behind your back and stretch your chest open.

abn.text: Interlace your fingers and push your palms toward the ceiling. Stretch!

abo.text: Hold your arms straight out to the sides. Make small circles. Burns faster than you'd think.

abp.text: Shake your hands out to release tension.

abq.text: Touch each fingertip to your thumb, making an O-shape.

abr.text: Make a fist, then fan your fingers out and stretch them wide.

abs.text: Make a fist, then spread your fingers like you're telling someone to stop.

abt.text: Squeeze each finger of your left hand with your right. Switch hands.

abu.text: Stretch your wrists — extend your arm, pull your fingers back gently.

abv.text: Rotate your wrists 10 times clockwise, then counterclockwise.

abw.text: Place your hand flat on the desk and gently spread your fingers apart.

abx.text: Tap your fingers on the desk one by one, pinky to thumb. Now reverse.

aby.text: Give yourself a hand massage. You've earned it.

abz.text: Stand up and stretch. Your spine has been waiting.

aca.text: Sit on the edge of your chair, twist your torso to one side, hold 10 seconds. Switch.

acb.text: Arch your back like a cat, then let it dip. Cat-cow stretch, office edition.

acc.text: Place both hands behind your lower back and gently arch backward.

acd.text: Stand with your back against the wall and slowly slide your arms up and down — wall angels.

acf.text: Stand up and do a lunge. Hold 10 seconds each leg.

acg.text: Stand up and do a few squats. Your chair is right there if things go wrong.

ach.text: Do 10 calf raises at your desk. Stealth fitness.

aci.text: Extend one leg straight out while seated. Hold 10 seconds. Switch.

acj.text: Roll your ankles in circles — clockwise, then counterclockwise.

ack.text: Point and flex your feet 10 times. Your ankles have been neglected.

acl.text: Stand on one foot for 30 seconds. Switch. Balance is a skill.

acm.text: Wiggle your toes inside your shoes. Yes, all of them.

acn.text: Stand up and march in place for 30 seconds.

aco.text: Do a few wall push-ups. Nobody's watching. Probably.

acp.text: Do 5 desk dips using the edge of your chair.

acq.text: Flex and release every muscle from your toes to your forehead. Full body reset.

acr.text: Scrunch your face tight for 5 seconds, then release. Facial tension: gone.

acs.text: Stand in a doorway and lean forward gently to stretch your chest.

act.text: Close your eyes and name the sounds you hear.

acu.text: Close your eyes and notice what comes to mind, without judgment.

acv.text: Think of something you're grateful for right now.

acw.text: Smile. You're alive and that's pretty cool.

acx.text: Take a mental snapshot of how your body feels. Any tension spots?

acy.text: Think of one nice thing you'd say to a friend, then say it to yourself.

acz.text: Notice 5 things in the room you never paid attention to before.

ada.text: Close your eyes and picture your happy place for 20 seconds.

adb.text: Put your phone face-down for 60 seconds. Nothing will happen. Promise.

adc.text: Your keyboard won't miss you. Stand up.

add.text: Your back just filed a formal complaint. Time to stretch.

ade.text: Look up from the screen. Plot twist: the world is 3D.

adf.text: Yawn. Even a fake one triggers a real one. Try it.

adg.text: Open your mouth wide, then close it slowly. Jaw tension: released.

adh.text: Hug yourself. Cross your arms and squeeze. Self-care isn't weird.

adi.text: Mini dance break — just 10 seconds. You know you want to.

adj.text: Pretend you're pulling a rope above your head. Side stretch unlocked.

adk.text: Press your palms together in front of your chest and hold. Namaste, coder.

adl.text: Massage your temples in small circles for 10 seconds. Instant calm.

adm.text: Your monitor called. It says you've been way too close for way too long.

adn.text: Your code won’t debug itself while you sit here. Actually, neither will it if you stand up. But at least your spine will forgive you.

ado.text: Explain your bug to an imaginary rubber duck. If that doesn’t work, explain it to the wall. Walls are great listeners.

adp.text: Your wrists have typed thousands of words today. Stretch them out — extend your arm and gently pull your fingers back.

adq.text: You’ve been holding an entire codebase in your head. Set it down for 20 seconds.

adr.text: Waiting for the build to finish? Perfect. Stand up and stretch. This is billable time.

ads.text: You have 47 unread Slack messages. They can wait 20 more seconds. Blink.

adt.text: “I’m too busy to take a break” is how you end up taking a much longer, involuntary one.

adu.text: Post-code-review brain is real. Close your eyes and let your neurons stop arguing.

adv.text: Writer’s block? Stand up. Walk 10 steps. Sit back down. The paragraph will fear your return.

adw.text: Decision fatigue is real. Stop choosing. Just breathe for 20 seconds.

adx.text: It’s the 3pm slump. Your blood sugar dipped. Stand up, stretch, and grab a snack.

ady.text: Your legs exist below your desk. Remind them by standing up.

adz.text: Your hip flexors have been in the fetal position for hours. Stand up and lunge.

aea.text: Your mid-back is stuck. Clasp your hands behind your head and gently arch backward.

aeb.text: Forearm stretch: extend your arm, palm up, and gently pull your fingers down. RSI prevention in 10 seconds.

aec.text: Next call, try walking while talking. Your brain works better in motion.

aed.text: Stairs exist. Climb some. Your cardiovascular system will send a thank-you card.

aee.text: Your screen brightness: is it matching the room, or is your face a flashlight? Adjust it.

aef.text: Blue light won’t ruin your life, but your screen is probably too bright. Dim it a notch.

aeg.text: Your headphones have been on for hours. Give your ears a break. They’re not designed for marathons.

aeh.text: Tonight’s sleep quality starts now. Look away from the screen and let your eyes rest.

aei.text: Reaching for chips? Try a handful of nuts instead. Your brain runs on better fuel than you think.

aej.text: Deep work is great. Deep isolation isn’t. When’s the last time you talked to a human?

aek.text: If you have a standing desk, now’s a good time to switch positions. If not, just stand up anyway.

ael.text: Seated twist: put your right hand on your left knee, twist, hold 10 seconds. Switch. Chair yoga, zero mat required.

aem.text: Is your room too warm? Cooler temperatures improve focus. Crack a window or adjust the thermostat.

aen.text: Take off your headphones. Listen to the actual sounds around you for 20 seconds.

aeo.text: You’ve been holding a mental model of the entire system in your head. That’s exhausting. Let it go for a moment.

aep.text: git commit -m "took a break". Best commit message you’ll write today.

aeq.text: Stack Overflow can’t help you stretch. Stand up. This is the one thing you have to do yourself.

aer.text: The deadline won’t move if you stretch for 20 seconds. But your vertebrae will. In a good way.

aes.text: Staring at the same paragraph for 10 minutes? Print it out and mark it up with a pen. Change the medium, change the perspective.

aet.text: Just shipped something? Submitted a draft? Stand up and do a victory stretch. You earned it.

aeu.text: Pre-deadline jitters? Move your body. Anxiety lives in stillness.

aev.text: Check your screen brightness. If you can see your reflection, it’s too bright for the room.

aew.text: Eat your snack away from the keyboard. Your crumbs don’t belong between the keys.

aex.text: A 5-minute walk generates more ideas than 30 minutes of staring at a blank page. Science says so.

aey.text: You have 38 tabs open. Close the ones you’ll never read. It’s not hoarding, it’s... okay, it’s hoarding.

aez.text: When you’ve read the same sentence five times and it still doesn’t make sense, that’s your brain saying: walk away.

afa.text: There is no Ctrl+Z for your spine. Stand up and take care of it now.

afb.text: Your second monitor can’t see you stretch. Go ahead, it won’t judge.

afc.text: Coffee is not a substitute for rest. But you knew that. Drink some water alongside it.

afd.text: The bug will still be there when you get back. But you’ll see it with fresh eyes.

afe.text: You just spent 10 minutes naming a variable. Your brain deserves a break.

aff.text: Meetings are over. Decompress. Roll your neck slowly left, then right.

afg.text: Your inbox will survive without you for 60 seconds. Look out a window.

afh.text: If your mouse hand is cramping, switch hands for a minute. It feels weird. That’s the point.

afi.text: Tingly fingers? That’s your nerves asking for a stretch. Wrist circles, 10 each direction.

afj.text: Been standing too long? Sit for a bit. The point is to alternate, not to suffer.

afk.text: Time to go AFK. Literally. Step Away From Keyboard.

afl.text: If you have a desk plant, check on it. If it’s dying, that’s a metaphor. Water both of you.

afm.text: Open a window. Fresh air does for your brain what a cold restart does for your computer.

afn.text: Put your chin to your chest and hold for 10 seconds. The back of your neck has been clenching all day.

afo.text: Squeeze your glutes while seated. Hold 5 seconds. Release. Nobody knows. Secret fitness.

afp.text: Seated hamstring stretch: extend one leg, reach for your toes, hold 10 seconds. Switch legs.

afq.text: Your eyes produce fewer tears when you focus on a screen. Blink slowly and deliberately 10 times.

afr.text: Deep breathing lowers blood pressure in real time. Breathe in for 4, out for 6. Repeat three times.

afs.text: Stand up and let gravity decompress your spine. Just hang your arms and breathe for 15 seconds.

aft.text: You know 200 keyboard shortcuts. Time to learn one body shortcut: stand, stretch, sit. Repeat.

afu.text: Switch your IDE to light mode for 5 minutes. Or dark mode. Change something. Reset the visual cortex.

afv.text: You’ve been staring at a blinking cursor. Now close your eyes and see nothing for 20 seconds. Luxury.

afw.text: Look out the window and find the farthest thing you can see. Focus on it. Your eye muscles needed that.

afx.text: Walk to the kitchen. Not for a reason. Just walk. Motion is the medicine.

afy.text: Find a stairwell and stretch your calves on the edge of a step. Hold 15 seconds each side.

afz.text: Your ears have been under headphones for hours. Take them off and enjoy the silence.

aga.text: Brain fog? That’s your prefrontal cortex running low. Stand up, move, and let it reboot.

agb.text: Multitasking is a myth. Your brain is just context-switching with overhead. Take a single-threaded break.

agc.text: Every context switch costs you 23 minutes to refocus. This break costs you 20 seconds. Do the math.

agd.text: Perfectionism is procrastination in a lab coat. Step away. Done is better than perfect.

age.text: Feeling like a fraud? Everyone does sometimes. Stand up and stretch — impostors don’t do self-care.

agf.text: Refreshing your email every 30 seconds isn’t productivity. Stand up. That’s productivity.

agg.text: Creative block? Change your physical position. New posture, new perspective.

agh.text: Your lower back has a complaint. Scoot to the edge of your chair and sit tall for 30 seconds.

agi.text: Shoulder pain is your body’s code review comment: “Needs changes.” Roll them backward 10 times.

agj.text: Wrist pain after coding? Make gentle fists and rotate slowly. 10 circles each direction.

agk.text: Cross one ankle over the opposite knee and lean forward. Hip opener. Hold 15 seconds. Switch.

agl.text: Look a coworker in the eye and say something nice. Human connection beats any notification.

agm.text: Listen to a nature sound for 30 seconds — rain, birds, ocean. Your nervous system will downshift.

agn.text: Deep focus is a sprint, not a marathon. You just sprinted. Walk it off.

ago.text: Posture check: are you leaning toward your screen like it owes you money? Sit back.

agp.text: Eat something. But taste it this time. Chew slowly. Your lunch break isn’t a speedrun.

agq.text: When did you last drink water? Not coffee. Water. Go.

agr.text: If there’s daylight available, get some on your skin. Your circadian rhythm is begging.

ags.text: Is your room too cold or too hot? Adjust it. Thermal comfort directly affects concentration.

agt.text: Box breathing: in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4. Your nervous system’s favorite loop.

agu.text: Raise your eyebrows as high as they go. Hold 5 seconds. Release. Your forehead was tenser than you thought.

agv.text: Spread your fingers as wide as you can. Hold 5 seconds. Now make a tight fist. Repeat three times.

agw.text: Engage your core while seated. Pull your belly button toward your spine and hold for 10 seconds.

agx.text: Stand on your toes for 10 seconds. Now rock back to your heels. Repeat. Micro-balance training.

agy.text: Notice your breathing. Don’t change it. Just notice. That’s mindfulness, and you just did it.

agz.text: This break reminder was written by a human who also ignores break reminders. Don’t be like us. Stretch.

aaa.title: Better together
aaa.text: Find it hard to take breaks alone? Try breaking with a coworker. You'll stick to it more and bond over shared complaints about deadlines. Studies show social breaks boost productivity.

aab.title: Step away
aab.text: Ever notice how your best ideas come in the shower? That's because your brain solves problems in the background. Step away from the screen and think about something completely unrelated.

aac.title: Microbreaks
aac.text: Short, frequent breaks reduce repetitive strain and keep your musculoskeletal system healthy. Think of them as maintenance for the human machine.

aad.title: Meditation
aad.text: Mindfulness meditation reduces anxiety, stress, and even physical pain. Not sure where to start? Even 5 minutes of focused breathing counts. There are dozens of free apps if you want guidance.

aae.title: Blink more
aae.text: You blink up to 66% less when staring at screens, which dries out your eyes. Blink rapidly for a few seconds to refresh your tear film. Your eyes do so much for you — return the favor.

aaf.title: Desk ergonomics
aaf.text: Monitor at eye level, keyboard at elbow height, feet flat on the floor. Bad ergonomics cause real damage over time. Spend 2 minutes checking your setup — your future self will thank you.

aag.title: Office workout
aag.text: You don't need a gym to move. March in place, do desk push-ups, or try some squats. Even 60 seconds of movement resets your energy levels.

aah.title: Switch it up
aah.text: If you have a standing desk or stability ball, now is a great time to switch. Alternating between sitting and standing reduces fatigue and keeps your muscles engaged.

aai.title: Read the signs
aai.text: Daydreaming? Trouble focusing? Re-reading the same line? These are your brain's polite way of saying: take a break already.

aaj.title: No-tech walk
aaj.text: Leave your phone behind and take a short walk. No podcasts, no music — just you and your thoughts. It's surprisingly refreshing in a world of constant input.

aak.title: The sitting problem
aak.text: Prolonged sitting increases your risk of heart disease, diabetes, and back problems. A 5-minute walk every hour can significantly offset these effects. Your body was built to move.

aal.title: Walking meetings
aal.text: Next time you have a one-on-one, suggest walking instead of sitting. Walking meetings boost creativity by up to 60%, according to Stanford research.

aam.title: Mindful snacking
aam.text: Grab a piece of fruit and eat it slowly. Notice the flavor, texture, and freshness. It's a mini meditation disguised as a snack.

aan.title: Coffee walk
aan.text: Going for coffee? Make it a 5-minute walk too. Two birds, one latte.

aao.title: Your brain on breaks
aao.text: An NIH study found that our brains rehearse and consolidate new skills during rest — not during practice. Breaks literally make you better at what you do.

aap.title: Move a little, gain a lot
aap.text: Even small amounts of regular exercise dramatically reduce stress and improve mood. You don't need an hour — 10 minutes of movement can shift your whole day.

aaq.title: Stretch routine
aaq.text: Found a set of stretches you like? Repeat them several times throughout the day. Consistency beats intensity when fighting the effects of prolonged sitting.

aar.title: Wrist circles
aar.text: Extend your arms with palms facing you, then slowly rotate your hands — 4 times clockwise, 4 times counterclockwise. Your wrists handle more stress than you think.

aas.title: Overhead reach
aas.text: Clasp your hands behind your head, then lift them up above your head with palms facing the ceiling. Hold for 10 seconds. Feel your back wake up.

aat.title: The 30/1 rule
aat.text: For every 30 minutes of sitting, get at least 1 minute of movement. Set a timer if you need to. Small habits compound into big health benefits.

aau.title: 7-minute workout
aau.text: A full-body workout in just 7 minutes. It's backed by science and requires no equipment. There are plenty of free apps to guide you through it.

aav.title: Elevate your heart rate
aav.text: Aim for 20 minutes of elevated heart rate (around 120 bpm), 4-5 times a week. It doesn't matter what you do — dance, jog, play with your dog. Your heart doesn't judge.

aaw.title: Take the stairs
aaw.text: Stair climbing is classified as vigorous exercise and burns more calories per minute than jogging. Next time, skip the elevator. Your legs will complain, but your heart will celebrate.

aax.title: Make something
aax.text: Art therapy is proven to reduce stress. Write a haiku, doodle a monster, take a photo of something beautiful. Creativity is a reset button for your brain.

aay.title: Declutter
aay.text: A messy desk correlates with higher stress. Take 5 minutes to organize your workspace. A clean space, a clear mind.

aaz.title: Eat outside
aaz.text: Nature exposure reduces cortisol, the stress hormone. When possible, take your lunch break outdoors. Even sitting near a window with a view of greenery helps.

aba.title: The power of yawning
aba.text: Yawning isn't just boredom — it cools your brain and produces tears that lubricate your eyes. Go ahead, fake a big yawn. Your body will make it real.

abb.title: Focus shifting
abb.text: Hold a finger close to your face and focus on it. Slowly move it away, then look far into the distance, then back. This exercises the muscles that control your eye's lens.

abc.title: Eye palming
abc.text: Cup your warm hands over your closed eyes and rest your elbows on the desk. Breathe slowly through your nose. Even 30 seconds of darkness gives your visual system a reset.

abd.title: Squeeze something
abd.text: Grab a stress ball, a pair of socks, or anything squeezable. Hold for 5 seconds, release, repeat. It relieves hand tension and feels oddly satisfying.

abe.title: Slow breathing
abe.text: Controlled slow breathing (around 6 breaths per minute) activates the parasympathetic nervous system, reducing blood pressure and anxiety. It's like a software update for your nervous system.

abf.title: Visualization
abf.text: Close your eyes and picture yourself in a calm place — a beach, a forest, a mountain top. Focus on the sounds, smells, and sensations. Mini mental vacation, zero travel costs.

abg.title: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding
abg.text: Feeling overwhelmed? Name 5 things you see, 4 you can touch, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste. This grounding technique pulls you back to the present moment.

abh.title: Power nap science
abh.text: A 10-20 minute nap boosts alertness and performance without grogginess. NASA found that pilots who napped for 26 minutes improved performance by 34%. If it's good enough for astronauts, it's good enough for you.

abi.title: The Pomodoro reset
abi.text: Work for 25 minutes, break for 5. After four rounds, take a longer break. The Pomodoro Technique isn't just a productivity hack — it's a sanity-preservation strategy.

abj.title: Doodle break
abj.text: Doodling during breaks actually improves concentration and memory retention by up to 29%, according to a study in Applied Cognitive Psychology. So grab a pen and let your hand wander.

abk.title: One song break
abk.text: Put on your favorite song and actually listen to it — not as background noise, but as the main event. Music activates the brain's reward system and reduces cortisol.

abl.title: Gratitude moment
abl.text: Write down 3 things you're grateful for right now. Studies show that a regular gratitude practice rewires your brain for positivity and reduces stress hormones.

abm.title: Cold water reset
abm.text: Splash cold water on your face or hold a cold glass against your wrists. The cold triggers your dive reflex, which slows heart rate and calms the nervous system instantly.

abn.title: Talk to a plant
abn.text: If you have a desk plant, check on it. Water it, turn it. If you don't have one, maybe it's time. Plants reduce stress and improve air quality. They're the perfect silent coworkers.

abo.title: Brain dump
abo.text: Grab a piece of paper and write down everything on your mind — tasks, worries, random thoughts. Getting it out of your head and onto paper frees up mental RAM.

abp.title: Pet your pet
abp.text: If you work from home with a pet, take a minute to pet them. Petting animals lowers cortisol and raises oxytocin. It's science-approved stress relief.

abq.title: Laugh therapy
abq.text: Watch a 2-minute funny video or read a few jokes. Laughter triggers endorphins, lowers stress hormones, and relaxes your muscles for up to 45 minutes.

abr.title: Fresh air fix
abr.text: Open a window or step outside for 60 seconds. Fresh air increases oxygen to your brain, improving concentration, serotonin levels, and energy.

abs.title: Body scan
abs.text: Starting from your toes, slowly move your attention up through your body. Notice where you're holding tension. Acknowledge it, breathe into it, and let it go.

abt.title: Desk yoga
abt.text: Seated cat-cow, spinal twist, forward fold — you can do yoga without leaving your chair. Your spine doesn't care about your outfit or location, it just wants to move.

abu.title: Read a page
abu.text: Keep a book nearby and read just one page during your break. Fiction transports your mind somewhere else. Non-fiction feeds it something new. Either way, you win.

abv.title: The 90-minute cycle
abv.text: Your brain works in 90-minute ultradian cycles of high and low energy. Working with these natural rhythms instead of against them makes you more productive and less exhausted.

abw.title: Curiosity break
abw.text: Look up one random fact about something that interests you. Learning something new during a break activates your brain's reward circuits differently than work does.

abx.title: Box breathing
abx.text: Breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4. Used by Navy SEALs to stay calm under pressure. If it works for them, it'll work for your inbox.

aby.title: Dance it out
aby.text: Put on a song and dance for the duration. Close the door if you must. Dancing releases endorphins, improves coordination, and makes you feel alive. Nobody looks cool dancing alone, and that's the point.

abz.title: Call someone
abz.text: Use your break to call someone you care about — just to say hi. Social connection is one of the strongest predictors of happiness and longevity.

aca.title: Sunlight dose
aca.text: Get 10-15 minutes of sunlight when possible. It regulates your circadian rhythm, boosts vitamin D production, and improves your mood. Your body is solar-powered too.

acb.title: Progressive relaxation
acb.text: Tense each muscle group for 5 seconds, then release. Start with your feet, move up to your calves, thighs, abs, hands, arms, shoulders, and face. Total tension release in under 3 minutes.

acc.title: Barefoot moment
acc.text: Take off your shoes and feel the floor under your feet. If you can, walk on grass. Grounding — or earthing — has been shown to reduce inflammation and improve sleep.

acd.title: Write to your future self
acd.text: Write a quick note to your future self — a goal, a wish, a reminder. It builds self-continuity and keeps you connected to what matters beyond today's to-do list.

ace.title: Digital declutter
ace.text: Close all the tabs you're not using. Unread notifications stacking up? Clear them. Digital clutter creates cognitive load, just like physical clutter.

acf.title: The 2-minute rule
acf.text: If something on your mind will take less than 2 minutes, do it now during your break. Clearing small tasks removes the mental weight of unfinished business.

acg.title: Posture audit
acg.text: Stand against a wall with your heels, butt, shoulders, and head touching it. That's what good posture feels like. Try to recreate that feeling when you sit back down.

ach.title: Scent break
ach.text: Smell something pleasant — coffee beans, a candle, essential oils, or fresh air. Olfactory input is directly connected to your emotional brain and can shift your mood instantly.

aci.title: Cloud watching
aci.text: If you can see the sky, spend a minute watching the clouds. It's the original screensaver — and it gives your brain the kind of soft focus that promotes creative thinking.

acj.title: Rubber duck wisdom
acj.text: Programmers use rubber ducks to explain code and find bugs. But the real magic? Stepping away from the problem entirely. Your subconscious keeps processing while you stretch. Come back and the solution is just... there.

ack.title: RSI is not a badge
ack.text: Repetitive Strain Injury affects up to 64% of computer workers. The early signs — tingling, stiffness, aching wrists — are easy to ignore and expensive to treat later. Stretch your forearms: extend your arm, palm down, and gently pull your fingers toward you. Hold for 15 seconds each side.

acl.title: The compile-time stretch
acl.text: Waiting for a build, deploy, or test suite? That’s not dead time — it’s free stretch time. Stand up, touch your toes (or try to), and roll back up slowly. Your code and your spine will both be ready when it finishes.

acm.title: Attention fragments
acm.text: The average knowledge worker checks email or messages every 6 minutes. Each check costs a context switch that takes 23 minutes to recover from. During this break, put your phone face-down and close your chat apps. Reclaim your attention span one break at a time.

acn.title: The busy paradox
acn.text: Research from Stanford shows that working without breaks doesn’t make you faster — it makes you slower, less accurate, and more likely to make mistakes you’ll spend even longer fixing. Taking breaks isn’t slacking. It’s engineering efficiency.

aco.title: Post-review recovery
aco.text: Just survived a code review? Or gave one? Either way, your brain has been in hypercritical mode. Time to shift gears. Stand up, shake out your hands, roll your shoulders, and let your brain switch from ‘judge mode’ to ‘rest mode.’

acp.title: Blank page, full body
acp.text: Writer’s block isn’t a creativity problem — it’s often a body problem. When you’re physically tense, your mind tightens too. Walk around for 5 minutes. Stretch your arms overhead. The words will come back, and they’ll be better.

acq.title: The 3pm crash
acq.text: That post-lunch energy dip is caused by your circadian rhythm, not just what you ate. Instead of reaching for caffeine, try a 5-minute walk or some light stretching. Movement boosts cortisol naturally and resets your alertness without the caffeine crash later.

acr.title: Dead legs syndrome
acr.text: Sitting compresses the blood vessels in your legs and reduces circulation. After 90 minutes of sitting, blood flow to the legs can drop by 50%. Stand up, walk around, or do 10 calf raises. Your legs — and your cardiovascular system — will thank you.

acs.title: Hip flexor SOS
acs.text: Your hip flexors shorten and tighten after prolonged sitting, pulling your pelvis forward and causing lower back pain. Try this: stand up, step one foot back into a lunge, and push your hips forward. Hold for 30 seconds each side. This is the most neglected desk-worker stretch.

act.title: Thoracic twist
act.text: Your thoracic spine (mid-back) gets locked up from hunching over a keyboard. Sit on the edge of your chair, cross your arms over your chest, and slowly rotate left and right. Hold each side for 10 seconds. You should feel things pop back into place.

acu.title: Forearm rescue
acu.text: Your forearms contain 20 muscles that control your fingers and wrists. After hours of typing and mousing, they’re exhausted. Extend one arm with your palm facing away, and gently pull your fingers back with the other hand. Hold 15 seconds. Switch. Repeat twice.

acv.title: Walk and talk
acv.text: Got a call coming up? Take it while walking. Stanford research found that walking boosts creative output by 60%. You don’t need a treadmill desk — just pace around your room or walk outside. Your ideas will be sharper and your body will thank you.

acw.title: Stair power
acw.text: Climbing stairs for just 3 minutes boosts energy more effectively than 30 milligrams of caffeine, according to a University of Georgia study. If you have access to a staircase, do a few laps during this break. It’s quick, free, and works every time.

acx.title: Screen and sleep
acx.text: Exposure to bright screens in the evening suppresses melatonin production by up to 50%. If it’s after 5pm, consider dimming your screen or enabling night mode. Your sleep tonight is being decided by what your eyes see right now.

acy.title: Blue light reality
acy.text: Blue light from screens probably won’t damage your retinas, but it does contribute to digital eye strain and can disrupt your sleep cycle. The fix isn’t expensive glasses — it’s looking away regularly, adjusting brightness, and taking breaks like this one.

acz.title: Ear fatigue
acz.text: Wearing headphones for more than 60 minutes at a time can cause ear fatigue, pressure buildup, and even hearing damage at high volumes. Take them off for this break. Let your ears breathe. If you must have sound, try speakers at a moderate volume for a while.

ada.title: Decision battery
ada.text: You make about 35,000 decisions a day, and each one depletes a finite resource. By afternoon, your decision quality drops significantly — this is ‘decision fatigue.’ During this break, stop choosing. Don’t scroll, don’t pick, don’t plan. Just be still.

adb.title: Stress snacking audit
adb.text: Stress eating isn’t about hunger — it’s about cortisol telling your brain it needs comfort. Next time you reach for a snack, pause and ask: am I hungry, or am I stressed? If stressed, try 5 deep breaths first. If still hungry after that, eat — but choose something that fuels you.

adc.title: The isolation trap
adc.text: Deep focus is essential for creative and technical work, but prolonged isolation raises cortisol and lowers oxytocin. Use this break to say hi to someone — a coworker, a neighbor, a family member. Even a brief social interaction resets your stress baseline.

add.title: Standing desk shuffle
add.text: Standing desks aren’t magic — standing still for hours is almost as bad as sitting still. The key is alternating. If you’ve been standing, sit for a bit. If sitting, stand. Shift your weight, wiggle your toes, or march in place. Movement, not position, is the goal.

ade.title: Chair yoga: seated pigeon
ade.text: Cross your right ankle over your left knee. Sit tall and gently lean forward until you feel a stretch in your right hip and glute. Hold for 30 seconds, then switch sides. This is one of the best hip-opening stretches you can do without leaving your chair.

adf.title: Temperature and focus
adf.text: Research from Cornell found that raising office temperature from 20°C to 25°C reduced typing errors by 44% and increased output by 150%. If you’re cold, warm up. If you’re too warm, cool down. Your thermostat is a productivity tool.

adg.title: Sound hygiene
adg.text: Constant background noise — open offices, notifications, music with lyrics — increases cognitive load by up to 66%. During this break, remove all audio. Sit in silence for 2 minutes. It might feel weird at first. That’s how you know you needed it.

adh.title: Codebase weight
adh.text: Holding a complex system in working memory is one of the most cognitively expensive tasks humans do. It’s why you feel drained after a day of ‘just sitting.’ Take this break to deliberately dump your mental state. Write down where you are, then let go.

adi.title: Git commit and stretch
adi.text: Before you push that commit, push yourself out of your chair. Make it a ritual: every commit = one stretch. Over a productive day, that’s 10-20 microbreaks built into your workflow. Your version history and your health history both improve.

adj.title: Words losing meaning
adj.text: There’s a psychological phenomenon called ‘semantic satiation’ — when you stare at a word so long it stops looking real. If you’ve been editing the same paragraph for 20 minutes, that’s your signal. Step away. When you return, the text will feel fresh and the errors will be obvious.

adk.title: The walk draft
adk.text: Many famous writers — Dickens, Beethoven, Darwin — took long daily walks as part of their creative process. You don’t need 2 hours. Even 5 minutes of walking shifts your brain from focused mode to diffuse mode, where creative connections happen.

adl.title: Deadline anxiety
adl.text: Pre-deadline stress triggers your fight-or-flight response, which narrows your thinking and increases errors. Paradoxically, the best thing you can do before a deadline is take a break. Movement metabolizes stress hormones and restores the broad thinking you need to finish strong.

adm.title: The submission ritual
adm.text: Just hit submit? Sent the email? Merged the PR? Don’t immediately start the next task. Give your brain a moment to register the completion. Stand up, stretch, maybe even celebrate. Acknowledging milestones — even small ones — prevents burnout.

adn.title: Glycemic rollercoaster
adn.text: That energy crash you feel mid-afternoon? It’s partly a blood sugar dip triggered by high-carb lunches. For sustained energy, pair carbs with protein and fiber. But right now, just move — a 5-minute walk stabilizes glucose levels and clears the fog.

ado.title: Numb legs protocol
ado.text: Tingling or numbness in your legs after sitting is caused by compressed nerves and reduced blood flow. Stand up and shake each leg for 10 seconds. Then do 10 marching-in-place steps. Blood flow restored, feeling returned, productivity resumed.

adp.title: Lighting audit
adp.text: Poor lighting causes eye strain, headaches, and fatigue. Your screen should be about the same brightness as your surroundings — not a glowing rectangle in a dark room. Adjust your desk lamp or room lights now. Your eyes will immediately feel the difference.

adq.title: Headphone break protocol
adq.text: Audiologists recommend the 60/60 rule: no more than 60% volume for no more than 60 minutes at a time. Your ears don’t have a pain threshold for gradual damage — hearing loss sneaks up on you. Take off your headphones for this entire break.

adr.title: Micro-workout
adr.text: You don’t need a gym. Right now, do 10 squats, 10 push-ups (or wall push-ups), and 10 calf raises. Total time: under 3 minutes. Total benefit: improved blood flow, elevated heart rate, boosted endorphins, and a smug sense of accomplishment.

ads.title: The printout trick
ads.text: Writers and editors: try printing your draft and reading it on paper. You’ll catch errors your screen-trained eyes miss. The physical act of holding paper and using a pen activates different cognitive pathways than screen editing. Old school? Yes. Effective? Absolutely.

adt.title: Spinal decompression
adt.text: Your spine compresses under gravity all day. Try this: stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, interlace your fingers above your head, and stretch as tall as you can. Hold for 15 seconds. You might actually be a centimeter or two taller right now.

adu.title: The attention tax
adu.text: Every notification, every badge, every unread message is a tiny tax on your attention. Over a day, these add up to hours of lost focus. During this break, turn off all notifications. When you return, you’ll have a full attention budget to spend on what matters.

adv.title: Wrist care station
adv.text: Your wrists handle about 40,000 keystrokes per day. Extend your right arm, palm facing the floor, and use your left hand to gently pull your fingers down and back. Hold 15 seconds. Switch. Then make slow fist-to-fan motions 10 times. Your tendons will thank you.

adw.title: The debug walk
adw.text: Studies at Stanford and other universities confirm that walking improves creative problem-solving by up to 60%. If you’re stuck on a bug or a design decision, stop staring at the screen. Walk for 5 minutes. The solution is more likely to appear when you’re not looking for it.

adx.title: Muscle memory reset
adx.text: Your body adapts to whatever position you hold longest. After hours of sitting, your muscles literally reshape around that posture. Stand up and do the opposite: arch your back, open your chest, reach overhead. Remind your muscles what ‘upright’ feels like.

ady.title: Eye muscle workout
ady.text: Your eyes have six muscles each, and staring at a fixed screen distance makes them stiff. Try this: hold a pen at arm’s length, focus on it, then shift focus to something 6 meters away. Alternate 10 times. It’s like stretching, but for your eyes.

adz.title: Brain rehearsal science
adz.text: Neuroscience shows your brain replays and consolidates skills during rest, not during practice. NIH researchers found that taking breaks led to faster skill acquisition. So this break isn’t procrastination — it’s literally how your brain gets better at what you just practiced.

aea.title: Snack with purpose
aea.text: If you’re going to snack, make it count. Nuts, dark chocolate, berries, and green tea all contain compounds that support focus and reduce inflammation. Skip the vending machine candy bar. Your brain runs best on real food, not sugar spikes.

aeb.title: The cortisol reset
aeb.text: Sitting in a stressed, hunched posture actually increases cortisol levels. Amy Cuddy’s research (debated but intriguing) suggests that expansive postures lower stress hormones. Stand up, put your hands on your hips, and stand tall for 2 minutes. Superman pose. No cape required.

aec.title: Micro-nap science
aec.text: A 6-minute nap improves memory consolidation, according to research from the University of Düsseldorf. You don’t need to fall asleep — just close your eyes and rest for a few minutes. Even the transition toward sleep activates memory-processing networks.

aed.title: Walking meditation
aed.text: Walk slowly and deliberately for 3 minutes. Focus on the sensation of each footstep — heel to toe, the shift of weight, the floor beneath you. This is walking meditation, and it combines the benefits of movement and mindfulness in one simple practice.

aee.title: Trigger point therapy
aee.text: Feel that knot between your shoulder blade and spine? That’s a trigger point in your rhomboid muscle. Press a tennis ball (or your fist) against it and apply firm pressure for 30 seconds. Release slowly. Do both sides. Office-grade muscle therapy, zero appointment needed.

aef.title: Screen distance check
aef.text: Your monitor should be about 50-70 centimeters from your eyes — roughly an arm’s length. Too close increases eye strain; too far makes you lean forward. Measure it now. If you’ve been slowly creeping toward your screen all day, push it back.

aeg.title: The creative detour
aeg.text: Neuroscience calls it ‘incubation’ — the phenomenon where stepping away from a problem lets your brain’s default mode network find solutions you couldn’t see while focused. Take a 5-minute break doing something completely unrelated. Doodle, stretch, or stare at clouds. Your brain is still working.

aeh.title: Circulation checkpoint
aeh.text: After 30 minutes of sitting, the rate of blood flow through your leg arteries decreases significantly. The fix is simple: stand up and walk for just 5 minutes. Studies show this is enough to restore normal blood flow and protect your vascular health.

aei.title: Jaw and TMJ relief
aei.text: Stress, concentration, and screen work often cause unconscious jaw clenching, which can lead to TMJ pain, headaches, and tooth damage. Open your mouth wide, hold for 5 seconds, then gently move your jaw left and right. Massage the muscles just below your ears in small circles.

aej.title: Hydration and brainpower
aej.text: Even mild dehydration (1-2% body weight) impairs concentration, increases perceived task difficulty, and worsens mood. Your brain is roughly 75% water. Drink 200-250 ml of water right now. Not coffee. Not soda. Water. Your neurons are parched.

aek.title: Tab bankruptcy
aek.text: If you have more than 20 browser tabs open, you’re not multitasking — you’re accumulating cognitive debt. Each open tab is an unresolved decision. During this break, declare tab bankruptcy. Close everything you won’t need in the next hour. The mental relief is immediate.

ael.title: Ulnar nerve check
ael.text: Do your pinky and ring finger tingle or go numb? That’s likely your ulnar nerve getting compressed at your elbow. Avoid resting your elbows on hard surfaces while typing. Straighten your arms fully, stretch them out, and shake your hands for 10 seconds.

aem.title: Wall stretch combo
aem.text: Stand facing a wall at arm’s length. Place both hands on the wall at shoulder height and lean forward, keeping your back straight. Hold for 15 seconds — that’s your chest. Now turn sideways, place one hand on the wall and rotate away from it. Hold 15 seconds each side. Chest and shoulders: opened.

aen.title: The focus dividend
aen.text: A DeskTime study of top-performing workers found the most productive pattern: 52 minutes of focused work followed by a 17-minute break. The break isn’t wasted time — it’s what makes the focused time actually focused. You’re investing in your next productive hour right now.

aeo.title: Vitamin D desk check
aeo.text: If you work indoors all day, you’re likely deficient in vitamin D — up to 42% of adults are. Vitamin D affects mood, immunity, and bone health. Step outside for 5 minutes if there’s sunlight. Your skin synthesizes vitamin D in as little as 10 minutes of sun exposure.

aep.title: Ankle mobility
aep.text: Your ankles support your entire body weight but rarely get stretched. Try this: stand on one foot and slowly trace the alphabet with the other foot. Yes, all 26 letters. Switch feet. It takes about 90 seconds per foot and dramatically improves ankle stability.

aeq.title: The procrastination paradox
aeq.text: Procrastination isn’t laziness — it’s an emotional regulation problem. You avoid tasks that trigger negative feelings (anxiety, boredom, self-doubt). A 5-minute break with physical movement can regulate those emotions enough to make starting feel possible again. Move first, motivate later.

aer.title: End-of-day wind-down
aer.text: Before you close your laptop, take 3 minutes to write down what you accomplished, what’s pending, and one thing you’re proud of. This ‘shutdown ritual’ creates cognitive closure, prevents work thoughts from invading your evening, and gives you a running start tomorrow.
